title: Data Structures and Algorithms Quiz
description: Check the key idea from each of the 28 DSA lessons. Use a small list or sketch to help you think. After the quiz, review the explanations and try again.

questions.question: A running total starts at 0 and adds 3, 1, and 4. What should it print?
questions.explanation: After each addition the total is 3, then 4, then 8. The last total is the answer.

questions.question: A Java example declares public class Main. What should its source file be called?
questions.explanation: Java matches a public class name to its file name. The class Main belongs in Main.java, including the capital M.

questions.question: A plan always reads only the first item of a non-empty array. Which growth label fits that work?
questions.explanation: The plan reads one item whether the array holds 2 items or 2,000. That amount of work stays constant.

questions.question: The scores are [4, 7, 2]. After replacing index 0 with 8, which scores remain?
questions.explanation: Index 0 is the first place. Replacing that item changes 4 to 8 and keeps the length at 3.

questions.question: You know only the head of a 100-node singly linked list. How do you reach its last node?
options: Follow next links from the head
questions.explanation: A linked list stores links, not an array of numbered places. You must follow the next links to reach the end.

questions.question: A stack holds 4 then 7, with 7 on top. You peek once. What remains?
questions.explanation: Peek only reads the top. It does not remove 7, so both items stay in the stack.

questions.question: Why does the short array queue move a head index forward?
options: To serve the front without shifting the remaining items
questions.explanation: The next item is already in the next array place. Moving head selects it without copying the whole line.

questions.question: Which task fits a set best?
options: Remember whether a card number has appeared
Remember exactly how many copies of each card appeared
Read the third item in a fixed row
questions.explanation: A set answers membership questions and removes duplicates. Counts need extra values, and positions are an array idea.

questions.question: A map stores key 4 with value 0. How can you distinguish this from a missing key?
options: Count the digits in the key
questions.explanation: Zero can be a real value. A membership check tells you whether the key is present, independent of that value.

questions.question: Why does a hash-table lookup compare the stored key after finding a slot?
options: Every key has the same value
Different keys can share a hash result
questions.explanation: The hash narrows the search but does not prove equality. Comparing the full key avoids returning another key's value.

questions.question: What happens when linear search looks for a missing value in a list of five items?
options: It checks only the middle item
questions.explanation: No early match lets the search stop. It checks all five items before reporting that the value is missing.

questions.question: The middle value is 6, but the target is 9. What should the shown binary search do next?
options: Keep the right half and exclude the middle
questions.explanation: In a sorted list, 6 and every item to its left are too small. Moving low to mid + 1 keeps only possible matches.

questions.question: What does sorting [4, 2, 4] in ascending order produce?
questions.explanation: Sorting changes order, not item count. Both copies of 4 remain, so the result is 2 4 4.

questions.question: Why can this bubble sort stop after a pass with no swaps?
options: Every checked neighbour pair is already in order
questions.explanation: No swaps means every pair in the unfinished part was in order. Earlier passes already finished the right end, so the whole list is sorted.

questions.question: Does this selection sort become O(n) when its input is already sorted?
options: Yes, it stops after one comparison
No, it still scans every unfinished part
Yes, because there are no items
questions.explanation: The loops still compare all candidates even when each smallest item is already in place. The comparison count remains O(n²).

questions.question: Why does insertion sort save the next item as key before shifting?
options: To make a second sorted list
To keep that value safe while other values overwrite positions
questions.explanation: Shifts copy values into new positions. The saved key preserves the item we still need to insert into the gap.

questions.question: Why does sumTo(n - 1) help this recursion stop for a positive whole number?
options: It makes each problem one smaller until n reaches 0
It removes the need for a base case
questions.explanation: Subtracting 1 moves a non-negative whole-number input toward 0. The base case can then return an answer.

questions.question: Why does this merge sort need an extra buffer?
options: To remember which numbers are missing
To build a merged part before copying it back
questions.explanation: Writing directly over values that have not been read could lose them. The buffer safely holds the merged order until it is copied back.

questions.question: Which input can give this last-pivot quick sort its O(n²) worst case?
options: No input; it is always O(n log n)
questions.explanation: On an already sorted list, the last value is largest. Each partition leaves a large unfinished left part, so the work adds up quadratically.

questions.question: Why does the pair loop use left < right instead of left <= right?
options: To use the middle item twice
To require two distinct item positions
questions.explanation: When left equals right, both markers refer to the same item. The strict comparison stops before that item could be counted twice.

questions.question: Why does the tree-sum function return 0 for an empty branch?
options: To stop recursion and add no value for a missing node
questions.explanation: An empty branch has nothing to add. Returning 0 stops that call and leaves the rest of the sum unchanged.

questions.question: What can happen to an ordinary BST after inserting already sorted values?
options: It can become a one-sided chain with O(n) search
questions.explanation: Without a balancing rule, each new larger value can go to the right of the previous one. The search path can grow to n nodes.

questions.question: Is [4, 9, 7] a valid min-heap stored in an array?
options: Yes, because 4 is no larger than either child
No, because heaps must have four items
questions.explanation: A min-heap orders parents against children. It does not require the whole array to be sorted.

questions.question: Does inorder traversal sort the values of every binary tree?
options: No, sorted output needs the binary search tree ordering rule
questions.explanation: Traversal follows existing links; it does not rearrange values. The output is sorted only when the tree already obeys the binary search tree rule.

questions.question: In an undirected graph, an edge joins 1 and 2. Which matrix cells need a 1?
options: Both row 1, column 2 and row 2, column 1
questions.explanation: An undirected edge works both ways. The matrix must show the connection in both directions.

questions.question: Which container gives BFS its nearby-first order?
questions.explanation: A queue serves earlier discoveries first. This finishes the current distance layer before moving to later layers.

questions.question: Does DFS always visit the closest unvisited node to the start next?
options: Yes, it visits by distance layers
No, it follows one path deeply before returning
Only when node names are numbers
questions.explanation: DFS can reach a distant node along one path while a nearby node is still waiting. BFS is the traversal that works in distance layers for unweighted links.

questions.question: Why is ways[0] set to 1 in this counting problem?
options: There is one empty sequence of moves
Every stair has only one route
questions.explanation: Making no moves is one valid plan for climbing zero stairs. This base answer lets routes starting with one or two stairs be counted correctly.
